Part 1: Geospatial Data Wrangling with R
This part is about preparing spatial data before analysis. I need to import the data, check the CRS, convert coordinate tables into spatial points, and do simple geoprocessing.

Load Packages

library(sf)
library(tidyverse)
library(tmap)
library(knitr)

tmap_mode("plot")



Data Used

data_files <- tibble(

An sf data frame is still a data frame. The special part is the geometry column. This makes it easy to use dplyr and spatial functions together.


Quick Plot with Base R

plot(st_geometry(mpsz))









plot(mpsz["PLN_AREA_N"])








The first plot only shows geometry. The second plot colours the polygons by planning area. This is good for a quick check.


Plot Multiple Layers Together

plot(st_geometry(mpsz), border = "grey70")
plot(st_geometry(preschool), add = TRUE, pch = 20, col = "red", cex = 0.35)








The pre-school points now sit on top of the planning subzones. This tells me the projection is working.


A Cleaner ggplot View

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = mpsz, fill = "grey96", color = "grey65", linewidth = 0.12) +
  geom_sf(data = cyclingpath, color = "#2c7fb8", linewidth = 0.25, alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_sf(data = preschool, color = "#de2d26", size = 0.25, alpha = 0.45) +
  coord_sf() +
  labs(
    title = "Planning Subzones, Cycling Paths, and Pre-Schools",
    subtitle = "The layers align after CRS transformation",
    caption = "Data: data.gov.sg and LTA DataMall"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








This plot is just a visual check. I use it to see whether points, lines, and polygons are in the correct place.

Geoprocessing Use Case 1: Cycling Path Buffer

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(
  cyclingpath,
  dist = 5,
  nQuadSegs = 30
)


buffer_cycling <- buffer_cycling %>%
  mutate(AREA = st_area(geometry))

sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

The buffer shows the land around the cycling paths. The distance is 5 metres, same as the demo idea in the course notes.


Clip Buffer by One Subzone

mpsz_selected <- mpsz %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST")

buffer_cycling_selected <- st_intersection(
  buffer_cycling,
  mpsz_selected
) %>%
  mutate(CLIPPED_AREA = st_area(geometry))


tibble(
  selected_subzone = mpsz_selected$SUBZONE_N,
  number_of_buffer_parts = nrow(buffer_cycling_selected),
  clipped_area_sqm = as.numeric(sum(buffer_cycling_selected$CLIPPED_AREA)),
  clipped_area_sqkm = as.numeric(sum(buffer_cycling_selected$CLIPPED_AREA)) / 1000000
) %>%

The st_intersects() result tells which pre-school points fall inside each polygon. lengths() turns that list into a count.


Derive Area and Density

mpsz <- mpsz %>%
  mutate(
    Area = st_area(geometry),
    `PreSch Density` = `PreSch Count` / as.numeric(Area) * 1000000
  )


summary(mpsz$`PreSch Density`)

  0.000   0.000   5.154   6.449  10.908  35.602 


Density is better than raw count for comparison. A small subzone and a large subzone can have the same count, but the meaning is not the same.


Histogram of Pre-School Density

hist(
  mpsz$`PreSch Density`,
  main = "Distribution of Pre-School Density",
  xlab = "Pre-schools per square kilometre",
  col = "#9ecae1",
  border = "white"
)









mpsz %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `PreSch Density`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#3182bd", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Pre-School Density",
    x = "Pre-schools per square kilometre",
    y = "Number of subzones"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








The histogram shows that many subzones have low density. A few compact residential areas have much higher density.


Map Pre-School Density

ggplot(mpsz) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = `PreSch Density`), color = "white", linewidth = 0.08) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", na.value = "grey90") +
  labs(
    title = "Pre-School Density by Planning Subzone",
    subtitle = "Number of pre-schools per square kilometre",
    fill = "Centres\nper sq km"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








This map is not from tmap, but it helps me check the derived variable before using it in later analysis.

Part 2: Choropleth Mapping with R
This part is about turning data into thematic maps. I use dependency ratio as the mapping variable.

Import Mapping and Population Data

mpsz2019 <- st_read(
  "data/geospatial/master_plan_2019_subzone_no_sea.geojson",
  quiet = TRUE
) %>%
  st_transform(3414)

clean_count <- function(x) {
  parse_number(na_if(as.character(x), "-"))
}

pop_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/aspatial/respop_subzone_age_sex_2020.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("Total_"), clean_count))


tibble(
  layer = c("Master Plan 2019 subzones", "Census 2020 population table"),
  records = c(nrow(mpsz2019), nrow(pop_raw)),
  columns = c(ncol(mpsz2019), ncol(pop_raw))
) %>%
  kable()

The course website uses a population table and a subzone layer. I use the same idea here with the downloaded local files.


Prepare Dependency Ratio

pop2020 <- pop_raw %>%
  filter(Number != "Total", !str_detect(Number, " - Total$")) %>%
  transmute(
    SUBZONE_N = str_to_upper(Number),
    YOUNG = Total_0_4 + Total_5_9 + Total_10_14,
    ECONOMY_ACTIVE = Total_15_19 + Total_20_24 + Total_25_29 +
      Total_30_34 + Total_35_39 + Total_40_44 + Total_45_49 +
      Total_50_54 + Total_55_59 + Total_60_64,
    AGED = Total_65_69 + Total_70_74 + Total_75_79 +
      Total_80_84 + Total_85_89 + Total_90andOver,
    TOTAL = Total_Total,
    DEPENDENCY = round((YOUNG + AGED) / ECONOMY_ACTIVE, 4)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(ECONOMY_ACTIVE), ECONOMY_ACTIVE > 0)

Some subzones are unmatched. This is normal because not every planning subzone is a residential area.


Quick Choropleth with qtm

qtm(mpsz_pop2020, fill = "DEPENDENCY")








qtm() is useful for a fast map. I use it when I only need a quick first look.


Choropleth with tm_shape and tm_polygons

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")








This is the basic tmap structure. tm_shape() gives the spatial object. tm_polygons() draws the polygons.


Use tm_fill and tm_borders

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(
    col = "grey60",
    lwd = 0.1,
    lty = "dashed"
  )








tm_polygons() is a shortcut for fill plus borders. I like the shortcut, but separating them helps me control the border style.


Built-In Classification Methods

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      n = 5
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal",
      n = 5
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "kmeans",
      n = 5
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Different classification methods can make the same data look different. This is why map classification is a design choice, not just a technical setting.


Custom Breaks

summary(mpsz_pop2020$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.2770  0.3885  0.4578  0.4540  0.5026  0.7833     130 



dependency_breaks <- c(0, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.80)

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      breaks = dependency_breaks
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








The website uses custom breaks too. I adjusted the break values because my downloaded population table gives a lower range.


ColourBrewer Palette

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      n = 5,
      values = "brewer.greens"
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      n = 5,
      values = "-brewer.greens"
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








The minus sign reverses the colour order. This changes which values get the darkest colour.


Cartographic Furniture

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      n = 5
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits(
    "Source: data.gov.sg",
    position = c("left", "bottom")
  )








Compass, scale bar, grid, and source note help the map read like a proper map output.


Map Legend and Layout

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      n = 5
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Dependency ratio"
    )
  ) +
  tm_pos_auto_in() +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits(
    "Source: data.gov.sg",
    position = c("left", "bottom")
  )








The legend title makes the mapped variable clearer. This is a small change, but it helps the reader.


Map Style

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      n = 5,
      values = "-brewer.greens"
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("natural")









tmap_style("white")

The style changes the overall look of the map. I reset it back to white after this demo.


Small Multiple Maps by Multiple Fill Variables

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")
    ),
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal",
      n = 5,
      values = "brewer.blues"
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("natural")








This creates small multiples from two variables. It is useful when I want to compare young and aged population patterns.

tmap_style("white")



Small Multiple Maps with tmap_arrange

youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "YOUNG",
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"),
      item.height = 0.8
    ),
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      values = "brewer.blues"
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of young population")

agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "AGED",
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"),
      item.height = 0.8
    ),
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      values = "brewer.blues"
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of aged population")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp = 1, ncol = 2)








This version builds two separate maps first. Then I arrange them side by side.


Small Multiple Maps with tm_facets

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      values = "brewer.blues"
    )
  ) +
  tm_facets(
    by = "REGION_N",
    nrow = 2,
    ncols = 3,
    free.coords = TRUE,
    drop.units = TRUE
  ) +
  tm_layout(
    legend.show = TRUE,
    title.position = c("center", "center"),
    title.size = 20
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Facets split the map by region. This makes regional comparison easier.


Select One Region

mpsz_pop2020 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      values = "brewer.greens"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend()
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








This map focuses only on the Central Region. It is clearer when the study area is small.


Add Statistical Chart and Outlier Highlight

mpsz_selected <- mpsz_pop2020 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")

mpsz_selected %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      values = "brewer.greens"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(),
    fill.chart = tm_chart_box()
  ) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)








The box chart gives a quick statistical view beside the map. It helps me see whether the mapped values have unusual cases.

stats <- boxplot.stats(mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out

outlier_vals

outlier_sf <- mpsz_selected[mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

outlier_sf %>%

Interactive Map

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2020 %>%

    "DEPENDENCY",

    )

This map is interactive. I can zoom, pan, and click a subzone to see the popup information.

Final Reflection
This hands-on exercise shows the full flow from raw data to maps. First, I prepare the spatial data and check the CRS. Then I create useful variables such as buffer area, pre-school density, and dependency ratio. Finally, I use different tmap options to show how map design can change the way a pattern is read.

Part 1: First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
First-order analysis is mainly about intensity. In simple terms, I am asking where child care services are more concentrated.

Import and Transform Geospatial Data

mpsz_sf <- st_read(
  "data/geospatial/master_plan_2019_subzone_no_sea.geojson",
  quiet = TRUE
) %>%
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

childcare_sf <- st_read(
  "data/geospatial/childcare_services.geojson",
  quiet = TRUE
) %>%
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)


layer_summary <- tibble(
  layer = c("mpsz_sf", "childcare_sf"),
  features = c(nrow(mpsz_sf), nrow(childcare_sf)),
  geometry_type = c(
    paste(unique(st_geometry_type(mpsz_sf)), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(st_geometry_type(childcare_sf)), collapse = ", ")
  ),
  epsg = c(st_crs(mpsz_sf)$epsg, st_crs(childcare_sf)$epsg)
)

kable(layer_summary)

EPSG:3414 uses metres. This matters because nearest neighbour distance and KDE bandwidth both depend on distance units.


Map the Child Care Services

tm_shape(mpsz_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey70", lwd = 0.3) +
  tm_shape(childcare_sf) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.03, col = "#2b8cbe", alpha = 0.55) +
  tm_title("Child Care Services in Singapore")








The points are not evenly spread across the island. They are mostly in residential planning areas, which is expected for this type of facility.


Convert sf Data to ppp

coords <- st_coordinates(childcare_sf)

childcare_ppp <- ppp(
  x = coords[, "X"],
  y = coords[, "Y"],
  window = as.owin(st_bbox(mpsz_sf))
)

class(childcare_ppp)

[1] "ppp"


The course uses as.ppp(childcare_sf). In my current spatstat setup, I create the same ppp object explicitly from the point coordinates.

tibble(
  total_points = npoints(childcare_ppp),
  duplicated_xy = sum(duplicated(as.data.frame(coords))),
  window_type = childcare_ppp$window$type
) %>%
  kable()




total_points

window_type

Some centres share the same coordinate. This can happen when several services are in the same building.


Create the Singapore Study Window

mpsz_cl <- st_union(st_geometry(mpsz_sf))
sg_owin <- as.owin(mpsz_cl)

class(sg_owin)

[1] "owin"



plot(sg_owin, main = "Singapore study window")








The owin object tells spatstat where the study area is. Without it, the point pattern would only know the rectangular bounding box.


Combine Points and Window

childcareSG_ppp <- unmark(childcare_ppp[sg_owin])

childcareSG_ppp

Planar point pattern: 1925 points
window: polygonal boundary
enclosing rectangle: [2667.54, 56396.44] x [15748.72, 50256.33] units



window_summary <- tibble(
  points = npoints(childcareSG_ppp),
  window_type = Window(childcareSG_ppp)$type,
  window_area_sqkm = spatstat.geom::area.owin(Window(childcareSG_ppp)) / 1000000,
  average_intensity_per_sqkm = intensity(childcareSG_ppp) * 1000000
) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

Now the point pattern is clipped to the Singapore boundary. This is the object used in the nearest neighbour and density analysis.


Clark-Evans Test

ce_global_z <- clarkevans.test(
  childcareSG_ppp,
  correction = "none",
  clipregion = NULL,
  alternative = "clustered"
)

ce_global_z


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.49444, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)


The Clark-Evans R value is below 1. This means the child care services are closer together than a random pattern.

ce_global_mc <- clarkevans.test(
  childcareSG_ppp,
  correction = "none",
  clipregion = NULL,
  alternative = "clustered",
  method = "MonteCarlo",
  nsim = 99
)

ce_global_mc


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.49444, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)


The Monte Carlo test gives the same broad conclusion. The observed pattern is more clustered than Complete Spatial Randomness.


Kernel Density Estimation

kde_SG_diggle <- density(
  childcareSG_ppp,
  sigma = bw.diggle,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian"
)

plot(kde_SG_diggle, main = "KDE of child care services, bw.diggle")








KDE turns point locations into a smooth surface. High values show places with stronger concentration of child care services.

bw <- bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp)
bw

   sigma 
295.4419 


The bandwidth controls how smooth the density surface is. A larger bandwidth makes a smoother map.


Rescale KDE Values

childcareSG_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(
  childcareSG_ppp,
  1000,
  "km"
)


kde_childcareSG_km <- density(
  childcareSG_ppp_km,
  sigma = bw.diggle,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian"
)

plot(kde_childcareSG_km, main = "KDE after rescaling to kilometres")








Rescaling makes the distance unit easier to read. The pattern is the same, but the bandwidth is now expressed in kilometres.


Compare Bandwidth Methods

bw_scott <- bw.scott(childcareSG_ppp_km)

bandwidth_table <- tibble(
  method = c("bw.CvL", "bw.scott x", "bw.scott y", "bw.ppl", "bw.diggle"),
  sigma_km = c(
    as.numeric(bw.CvL(childcareSG_ppp_km)),
    as.numeric(bw_scott["sigma.x"]),
    as.numeric(bw_scott["sigma.y"]),
    as.numeric(bw.ppl(childcareSG_ppp_km)),
    as.numeric(bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp_km))
  )
) %>%
  mutate(sigma_km = round(sigma_km, 3))

Different methods choose different bandwidths. I keep bw.diggle for most maps because it gives a clear local pattern without being too rough.

kde_childcareSG_ppl <- density(
  childcareSG_ppp_km,
  sigma = bw.ppl,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian"
)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(kde_childcareSG_km, main = "bw.diggle")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ppl, main = "bw.ppl")







par(old_par)

bw.ppl uses a larger bandwidth here, so the density surface is smoother. bw.diggle keeps more local detail.


Compare Kernel Methods

sigma_km <- as.numeric(bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp_km))

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(
  density(childcareSG_ppp_km, sigma = sigma_km, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"),
  main = "Gaussian"
)
plot(
  density(childcareSG_ppp_km, sigma = sigma_km, edge = TRUE, kernel = "epanechnikov"),
  main = "Epanechnikov"
)
plot(
  density(childcareSG_ppp_km, sigma = sigma_km, edge = TRUE, kernel = "quartic"),
  main = "Quartic"
)
plot(
  density(childcareSG_ppp_km, sigma = sigma_km, edge = TRUE, kernel = "disc"),
  main = "Disc"
)







par(old_par)

Changing the kernel changes the surface shape slightly. The main hotspot pattern remains similar.


Fixed and Adaptive KDE

kde_childcareSG_fb <- density(
  childcareSG_ppp_km,
  sigma = 0.6,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian"
)

kde_childcareSG_ab <- adaptive.density(
  childcareSG_ppp_km,
  method = "kernel"
)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(kde_childcareSG_fb, main = "Fixed bandwidth, 0.6 km")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ab, main = "Adaptive bandwidth")







par(old_par)

Fixed bandwidth uses one smoothing distance everywhere. Adaptive bandwidth changes the smoothing by local point density.


Cartographic KDE Map

kde_childcareSG_terra <- terra::rast(kde_SG_diggle)
crs(kde_childcareSG_terra) <- "EPSG:3414"

kde_childcareSG_terra

I use the metre-based KDE here so the raster coordinates match EPSG:3414.

tm_shape(kde_childcareSG_terra) +
  tm_raster(
    col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "viridis"),
    col.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Density values",
      title.size = 0.7,
      text.size = 0.7,
      bg.color = "white",
      bg.alpha = 0.75,
      position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"),
      frame = TRUE
    )
  ) +
  tm_compass() +
  tm_layout(scale = 1.0)








This is a cleaner map output. It shows the KDE result as a raster surface instead of a basic R plot.


First-order Analysis by Planning Area

make_area_window <- function(planning_area) {
  mpsz_sf %>%
    filter(PLN_AREA_N == planning_area) %>%
    st_geometry() %>%
    st_union() %>%
    as.owin()
}

make_area_area <- function(planning_area) {
  mpsz_sf %>%
    filter(PLN_AREA_N == planning_area) %>%
    st_geometry() %>%
    st_union() %>%
    st_area() %>%
    as.numeric()
}

pg_owin <- make_area_window("PUNGGOL")
tm_owin <- make_area_window("TAMPINES")
ck_owin <- make_area_window("CHOA CHU KANG")
jw_owin <- make_area_window("JURONG WEST")

childcare_pg_ppp <- unmark(childcare_ppp[pg_owin])
childcare_tm_ppp <- unmark(childcare_ppp[tm_owin])
childcare_ck_ppp <- unmark(childcare_ppp[ck_owin])
childcare_jw_ppp <- unmark(childcare_ppp[jw_owin])


planning_area_summary <- tibble(
  planning_area = c("Punggol", "Tampines", "Choa Chu Kang", "Jurong West"),
  childcare_points = c(
    npoints(childcare_pg_ppp),
    npoints(childcare_tm_ppp),
    npoints(childcare_ck_ppp),
    npoints(childcare_jw_ppp)
  ),
  area_sqkm = c(
    make_area_area("PUNGGOL"),
    make_area_area("TAMPINES"),
    make_area_area("CHOA CHU KANG"),
    make_area_area("JURONG WEST")
  ) / 1000000
) %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqkm = round(area_sqkm, 2),
    points_per_sqkm = round(childcare_points / area_sqkm, 2)
  )

childcare_pg_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_pg_ppp, 1000, "km")

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: Spatial Point Pattern Analysis
section: Part 2: Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
Part 2: Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
Second-order analysis looks at distance relationships between points. Here I use Choa Chu Kang and Tampines because they have enough child care points and the course also uses them.






Note



The course uses 999 simulations for some CSR tests. I use simulation_n <- 99 so the page can render faster. The code structure is the same, and a larger number can be used for a final statistical run.



simulation_n <- 99
gf_rmax <- 500
kl_rmax <- 1000


G-function
The G-function looks at nearest neighbour distance from each observed point. If the observed curve rises faster than the CSR curve, nearby points are common.

G_CK <- Gest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "border", rmax = gf_rmax)
G_tm <- Gest(childcare_tm_ppp, correction = "best", rmax = gf_rmax)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(G_CK, xlim = c(0, gf_rmax), main = "G-function: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(G_tm, xlim = c(0, gf_rmax), main = "G-function: Tampines")







par(old_par)

The two plots show how quickly each child care centre finds another nearby centre.

G_CK_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_ck_ppp,
  Gest,
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rmax = gf_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

G_tm_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_tm_ppp,
  Gest,
  correction = "all",
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rmax = gf_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(G_CK_csr, main = "CSR envelope: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(G_tm_csr, main = "CSR envelope: Tampines")







par(old_par)

The envelope is the random benchmark. When the observed line moves outside the envelope, the pattern is not behaving like CSR at that distance.


F-function
The F-function uses random empty locations and measures the distance to the nearest child care point. It helps describe empty space.

F_CK <- Fest(childcare_ck_ppp, rmax = gf_rmax)
F_tm <- Fest(childcare_tm_ppp, correction = "best", rmax = gf_rmax)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(F_CK, main = "F-function: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(F_tm, main = "F-function: Tampines")







par(old_par)

If the F curve rises quickly, most places are close to a child care service. This is about coverage from the empty-space side.

F_CK_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_ck_ppp,
  Fest,
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rmax = gf_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

F_tm_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_tm_ppp,
  Fest,
  correction = "all",
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rmax = gf_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(F_CK_csr, main = "CSR envelope: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(F_tm_csr, main = "CSR envelope: Tampines")







par(old_par)

This adds a random reference to the empty-space analysis. It is useful because a visual curve alone can be hard to judge.


K-function
The K-function counts neighbours within increasing distance bands. It is useful for checking clustering across many distances.

K_ck <- Kest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley", rmax = kl_rmax)
K_tm <- Kest(childcare_tm_ppp, correction = "Ripley", rmax = kl_rmax)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(K_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)", main = "K-function: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(K_tm, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)", main = "K-function: Tampines")







par(old_par)

The transformed plot makes it easier to compare the observed pattern with the CSR reference line.

K_ck_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_ck_ppp,
  Kest,
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rank = 1,
  global = TRUE,
  rmax = kl_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

K_tm_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_tm_ppp,
  Kest,
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rank = 1,
  global = TRUE,
  rmax = kl_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(K_ck_csr, . - theo ~ r, main = "K CSR: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(K_tm_csr, . - theo ~ r, main = "K CSR: Tampines")







par(old_par)

For K-function envelopes, a line above the random envelope suggests clustering at that distance range.


L-function
The L-function is a transformed version of K. It is often easier to read because CSR is shown around zero after subtracting distance.

L_ck <- Lest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley", rmax = kl_rmax)
L_tm <- Lest(childcare_tm_ppp, correction = "Ripley", rmax = kl_rmax)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(L_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "L(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)", main = "L-function: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(L_tm, . - r ~ r, ylab = "L(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)", main = "L-function: Tampines")







par(old_par)

L-function is easier to explain visually. Values above zero usually indicate clustering.

L_ck_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_ck_ppp,
  Lest,
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rank = 1,
  global = TRUE,
  rmax = kl_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

L_tm_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_tm_ppp,
  Lest,
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rank = 1,
  global = TRUE,
  rmax = kl_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(L_ck_csr, . - theo ~ r, main = "L CSR: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(L_tm_csr, . - theo ~ r, main = "L CSR: Tampines")







par(old_par)

The CSR envelopes help confirm that the pattern is not only a visual impression. The services show clustering at short distances, especially in denser residential parts.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: Spatial Point Pattern Analysis
text:
Final Reflection
This hands-on exercise shows two ways to study point patterns. First-order methods show where the intensity is high. Second-order methods check how points relate to other points across distance. For child care services, clustering is expected because centres follow housing estates and population demand. The main limitation is that CSR is a simple benchmark, so the result should be read as an exploratory test rather than a full explanation of why centres are located there.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
This page follows Chapter 6: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis.
The chapter studies forest fire points in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung, Indonesia. To keep the data size small, I use a light subset of Indonesia 2023 active fire detections and only keep the records around Bangka Belitung.
The main question is simple:

Are fire points randomly distributed in space and time?
If not, where and when do they cluster?







Note



The full chapter uses sparr::spattemp.density() and stpp. For this submission, I use a lighter spatstat workflow so the page can render reliably. The idea is the same: combine point locations with their event time.

Part 4: STKDE by Month
The course computes spatio-temporal KDE. Here I use a lightweight version: split the points by month and compute a KDE for each month using the same spatial bandwidth.

  month_ppp <- unmark(fire_by_month[[current_month]])
  month_kde <- density(
    month_ppp,
    sigma = space_bandwidth,
    edge = TRUE
  )

  tibble(
    month = current_month,
    points = npoints(month_ppp),
    max_density = max(month_kde$v, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(max_density = signif(max_density, 3))

section: Part 5: STKDE by Day of Year
text:
Part 5: STKDE by Day of Year
Month is useful, but it is also coarse. I use day-of-year and a temporal weighting idea to create a few smoother time slices.

Temporal Weighted KDE Function

st_kde_slice <- function(target_day, lambda_days = 14, sigma = space_bandwidth) {
  temporal_weights <- dnorm(
    (marks(fire_yday_owin) - target_day) / lambda_days
  )

  density(
    unmark(fire_yday_owin),
    sigma = sigma,
    weights = temporal_weights,
    edge = TRUE
  )
}

The spatial bandwidth is 15 km. The temporal bandwidth is 14 days. So each output surface is mainly influenced by fires near the selected date.


Plot Day-of-Year KDE Slices

Part 6: Simple Space-Time Interaction Check
The full stpp workflow computes a formal space-time K-function. Here I make a simpler check by counting point pairs that are close in both space and time.

Pair Distance Summary

xy <- st_coordinates(fire_sf)
day_vec <- fire_sf$DayofYear

spatial_dist <- as.matrix(dist(xy)) / 1000
temporal_dist <- abs(outer(day_vec, day_vec, "-"))

upper_index <- upper.tri(spatial_dist)
space_pairs_km <- spatial_dist[upper_index]
time_pairs_days <- temporal_dist[upper_index]

total_pairs <- length(space_pairs_km)

interaction_table <- expand_grid(
  space_km = c(5, 10, 20),
  time_days = c(7, 14, 30)
) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    pair_count = sum(space_pairs_km <= space_km & time_pairs_days <= time_days),
    pair_share = pair_count / total_pairs
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(pair_share = round(pair_share, 4))

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
Final Reflection
This hands-on exercise extends point pattern analysis from space into space-time. I first prepare the study window and fire points, then use month and day-of-year as temporal marks. The monthly KDE shows when the fire activity becomes stronger. The day-of-year weighted KDE gives smoother time slices. The pair-distance table is a simple check that many fires happen near other fires in both space and time. Overall, the pattern is not just spatial. It also changes clearly through the year.
